items.q: All of the following are absolute (uremic) indications for dialysis EXCEPT:
items.exp: Absolute uremic indications: encephalopathy, halitosis, pruritis, pericarditis, bleeding and gastritis. Volume overload is a relative indication, along with hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis resistant to treatment. (Book p780)

items.q: Fill up: The absolute indications for dialysis in RPGN are all ______ in nature.
items.exp: Absolute indications for dialysis = uremic: encephalopathy, halitosis, pruritis, pericarditis, bleeding, gastritis. (Book p780)

items.q: Match the dialysis indications in RPGN with their category — 1) Absolute indication  2) Relative indication  3) Qualifier for the relative group … A) Resistant to treatment  B) Uremic encephalopathy, halitosis, pruritis, pericarditis, bleeding, gastritis  C) Volume overload, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis
items.exp: Absolute (uremic) indications: encephalopathy, halitosis, pruritis, pericarditis, bleeding and gastritis. Relative indications: volume overload, hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis, all qualified as resistant to treatment. (Book p780)

items.q: Hyperkalaemia in RPGN is an absolute indication for dialysis regardless of whether it responds to medical treatment.
opts: False — hyperkalaemia is a relative indication and must be resistant to treatment
True — hyperkalaemia is always an absolute uremic indication
True, but only if the ECG is normal
False — dialysis is never indicated for hyperkalaemia
items.exp: Hyperkalaemia appears along with volume overload and metabolic acidosis under relative indications, qualified as resistant to treatment. (Book p780)

items.q: On the basis of immunofluorescence, RPGN is classified into:
opts: Three types — I, II and III
Two types — granular and linear only
Four types — I, II, III and IV
Five types including double-positive and double-negative
items.exp: The TYPES flowchart of RPGN begins 'on the basis of immunofluorescence' and branches into type I (Goodpasture syndrome), type II (immune complex) and type III (pauci-immune). Types IV/V appear only inside the later double-positive vs double-negative table. (Book p780)

items.q: Type I RPGN is also known as:
items.exp: Type I / Goodpasture syndrome: IF shows linear IgG ± C3 in the capillary wall. (Book p780)

items.q: Fill up: Type I RPGN shows ______ IgG ± C3 in the capillary wall on immunofluorescence.
items.exp: Type I RPGN (Goodpasture syndrome) IF: linear IgG ± C3 in the capillary wall. (Book p780)

items.q: Match each RPGN type with its label in the immunofluorescence flowchart — 1) Type II  2) Type III  3) Type II age note … A) Commonest below 20 years  B) Immune complex deposition  C) Pauci-immune, the commonest type
items.exp: Type II = immune complex deposition (commonest in those below 20 years); type III = pauci-immune, marked m/c i.e. the commonest type overall. (Book p780)

items.q: Type II RPGN is commonest in patients:
items.exp: Type II RPGN is annotated 'm/c in <20 yrs age' within the immune-complex branch. (Book p780)

items.q: A 16-year-old girl has RPGN with immune-complex deposition on biopsy. Which example fits the book's type II list best?
items.exp: Type II (immune complex) examples: SLE — underlined as the most important cause — Henoch–Schönlein purpura, IPGN (IgA predominant) and membranoproliferative GN (10%). (Book p780)

items.q: Systemic lupus erythematosus is marked as the most important cause within the type II RPGN examples.
opts: False — HSP is the most important cause
False — MPGN is the most important cause
True, but only above 60 years of age
items.exp: In the type II branch, SLE is underlined with the note '(most important cause)'; HSP, IPGN (IgA predominant) and MPGN (10%) complete the list. (Book p780)

items.q: Which example does NOT belong to the type II (immune complex) group of RPGN?
items.exp: Microscopic polyangiitis belongs to type III (pauci-immune) with ANCA vasculitis and Wegener's granulomatosis. (Book p780)

items.q: Match each type II (immune-complex) RPGN example with the note printed beside it — 1) Systemic lupus erythematosus  2) Henoch-Schönlein purpura and IPGN  3) Membranoproliferative GN … A) Adult variety  B) 10%  C) Most important cause
items.exp: In the type II list SLE carries '(most important cause)', HSP with IPGN is bracketed as the adult variety, and MPGN is annotated 10%. (Book p780)

items.q: Type III RPGN is described as:
opts: Immune complex disease — commonest below 20 years
A disease seen only in children
items.exp: Type III (pauci-immune) is marked m/c, i.e. the commonest type of RPGN, with examples ANCA vasculitis, Wegener's granulomatosis and microscopic polyangiitis. (Book p780)

items.q: Which of these is NOT among the examples of type III (pauci-immune) RPGN?
items.exp: IPGN (IgA predominant) is listed under type II immune-complex RPGN; type III pauci-immune examples are ANCA vasculitis, Wegener's granulomatosis and microscopic polyangiitis. (Book p780)

items.q: Match the serology with its type in the double-positive versus double-negative table — 1) Anti-GBM + and ANCA +  2) Anti-GBM - and ANCA -  3) Prognosis of the double-positive type … A) Type V  B) Type IV  C) Good
items.exp: Type IV is double positive (anti-GBM +, ANCA +) with a good prognosis; type V is double negative (anti-GBM -, ANCA -) with a poor prognosis. (Book p780)

items.q: Prognosis is good in double-positive (type IV) RPGN and poor in double-negative (type V) RPGN.
opts: False — prognosis is poor in type IV and good in type V
False — prognosis is identical in both
True, but only when C3 is low
items.exp: The table's prognosis row reads good for type IV (double positive) and poor for type V (double negative). (Book p780)

items.q: A patient with RPGN has both anti-GBM antibody and ANCA positive on serology. According to the table he has:
opts: Type IV RPGN — with a good prognosis
Type V RPGN — with a poor prognosis
Type I RPGN — with a poor prognosis
Type III RPGN — with a poor prognosis
items.exp: Type IV = double positive (anti-GBM + and ANCA +), and this carries a good prognosis; type V (double negative) has a poor prognosis. (Book p780)
